title: 216. Algebra, Equations & Inequalities: Solving Equations Using Logarithm Laws
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations using the product law
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by applying the product law and checking the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_2 x+\log_2 4=5\).
questions.explanation: Using the product law, \(\log_2 x+\log_2 4=\log_2(4x)\). The equation becomes \(\log_2(4x)=5\). Convert to exponential form: \(4x=2^5=32\). Thus \(x=8\). The domain requires \(x>0\), and \(8>0\), so the solution is valid.
questions.hint: Combine the logarithms using the product law, then convert the equation to exponential form.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations using the product law
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation with two variable factors by applying the product law and domain restrictions.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_2(x+1)+\log_2(x-1)=3\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x+1>0\) and \(x-1>0\), so \(x>1\). Combine the logarithms:
\[
\log_2[(x+1)(x-1)]=3
\]
Then \((x+1)(x-1)=2^3=8\), so \(x^2-1=8\). Thus \(x^2=9\), giving \(x=3\) or \(x=-3\). Since the domain requires \(x>1\), only \(x=3\) is valid.
questions.hint: Apply the product law, solve the resulting quadratic, and reject any value that does not satisfy the domain.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations using the quotient law
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by applying the quotient law and checking the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log(x+3)-\log(x-1)=1\).
questions.explanation:
The base of \(\log\) is \(10\). The domain requires \(x+3>0\) and \(x-1>0\), so \(x>1\). Using the quotient law:
\[
\log\frac{x+3}{x-1}=1
\]
Then \(\frac{x+3}{x-1}=10\), so \(x+3=10x-10\). This gives \(13=9x\), so \(x=\frac{13}{9}\). Since \(\frac{13}{9}>1\), the solution is valid. The value \(x=1\) is not in the domain.
questions.hint: Use the quotient law to write the left side as a single logarithm, then solve the resulting equation.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations using the quotient law
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by combining logarithms with the quotient law and applying the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_2(x+5)-\log_2(x-1)=2\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x+5>0\) and \(x-1>0\), so \(x>1\). Using the quotient law:
\[
\log_2\frac{x+5}{x-1}=2
\]
Then \(\frac{x+5}{x-1}=2^2=4\), so \(x+5=4(x-1)=4x-4\). This gives \(9=3x\), so \(x=3\). Since \(3>1\), the solution is valid. The value \(x=1\) is not in the domain.
questions.hint: Combine the logarithms with the quotient law, then solve the resulting linear equation.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations using the power law
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by applying the power law and checking the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(2\log_3 x=4\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x>0\). Divide both sides by \(2\):
\[
\log_3 x=2
\]
Convert to exponential form: \(x=3^2=9\). Since \(9>0\), the solution is valid. The value \(x=81\) would satisfy \(\log_3 x=4\), not \(\log_3 x=2\).
questions.hint: Isolate the logarithm first, then convert the logarithmic equation to exponential form.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations using the product law
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation with quadratic arguments by using the product law and domain restrictions.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_5(x-2)+\log_5(x+2)=1\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x-2>0\) and \(x+2>0\), so \(x>2\). Using the product law:
\[
\log_5[(x-2)(x+2)]=1
\]
Then \((x-2)(x+2)=5^1=5\), so \(x^2-4=5\). Thus \(x^2=9\), giving \(x=3\) or \(x=-3\). Since the domain requires \(x>2\), only \(x=3\) is valid.
questions.hint: Combine the logarithms using the product law, solve the quadratic, and check the domain.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations using the product law
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation with a difference of squares by applying the product law.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_2(x+3)+\log_2(x-3)=4\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x+3>0\) and \(x-3>0\), so \(x>3\). Using the product law:
\[
\log_2[(x+3)(x-3)]=4
\]
Then \((x+3)(x-3)=2^4=16\), so \(x^2-9=16\). Thus \(x^2=25\), giving \(x=5\) or \(x=-5\). Since the domain requires \(x>3\), only \(x=5\) is valid.
questions.hint: Apply the product law, simplify the difference of squares, and reject values outside the domain.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations using the quotient law
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by combining logarithms with the quotient law and solving for \(x\).
questions.question: Solve \(\log_4(x+1)-\log_4(x-2)=1\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x+1>0\) and \(x-2>0\), so \(x>2\). Using the quotient law:
\[
\log_4\frac{x+1}{x-2}=1
\]
Then \(\frac{x+1}{x-2}=4^1=4\), so \(x+1=4(x-2)=4x-8\). This gives \(9=3x\), so \(x=3\). Since \(3>2\), the solution is valid.
questions.hint: Combine the logarithms with the quotient law, then solve the resulting equation and check the domain.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations using the product law
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation with a quadratic argument and apply domain restrictions.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_2 x+\log_2(x-6)=4\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x>0\) and \(x-6>0\), so \(x>6\). Using the product law:
\[
\log_2[x(x-6)]=4
\]
Then \(x(x-6)=2^4=16\), so \(x^2-6x-16=0\). Factor:
\[
(x-8)(x+2)=0
\]
so \(x=8\) or \(x=-2\). Since the domain requires \(x>6\), only \(x=8\) is valid.
questions.hint: Combine the logarithms with the product law, solve the quadratic, and check the domain condition \(x>6\).

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations using the product law
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by applying the product law and rejecting an extraneous solution.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_3(x+4)+\log_3(x-4)=2\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x+4>0\) and \(x-4>0\), so \(x>4\). Using the product law:
\[
\log_3[(x+4)(x-4)]=2
\]
Then \((x+4)(x-4)=3^2=9\), so \(x^2-16=9\). Thus \(x^2=25\), giving \(x=5\) or \(x=-5\). Since the domain requires \(x>4\), only \(x=5\) is valid. The value \(x=-5\) is extraneous.
questions.hint: Combine the logarithms, solve the resulting equation, and reject any candidate that violates the domain.
